Patient Vignette: Daniel (Age 36)

Daniel is a 36-year-old retail worker who has been married to his wife, Sarah, for nine years. They have two children, ages six and four. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown increasingly concerned about his irritability and emotional withdrawal over the past eighteen months.

The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late November. Daniel was working his usual shift at a large home improvement store, stocking shelves in the paint aisle. He remembers the fluorescent lights humming overhead, the smell of latex and turpentine, and the distant sound of a forklift. Then came the crash—a deafening, metallic groan followed by the shattering of glass and concrete. A section of the store’s roof, weakened by a construction error on a neighboring building, had collapsed. Daniel was forty feet away. He saw the cloud of dust, heard the screams, and watched a young coworker named Marcus disappear under a beam.

Daniel ran toward the rubble, pulling at debris with his bare hands until his manager physically restrained him. He remembers the sirens, the shouting, the feeling of dust coating his tongue. Three people were killed that day, including Marcus. Daniel was not physically injured, but he has never stopped seeing Marcus’s face, frozen in that split second before the beam fell.

In the weeks after, Daniel couldn’t stop thinking about it. He replayed the sequence obsessively, wondering if he could have done something differently—if he had called out, if he had been standing closer. He started having trouble sleeping. Every time he closed his eyes, he heard the crash. He began checking the ceilings in every room he entered, scanning for cracks or sagging drywall. At work, he now avoids the paint aisle entirely. He requested a transfer to the garden center, but the smell of fresh lumber still makes his stomach tighten.

His wife, Sarah, says he is not the same man she married. He used to be patient with their children, reading them bedtime stories and building pillow forts. Now he snaps at them for the smallest things—a spilled drink, a loud laugh. He has stopped going to family gatherings. Crowds feel dangerous. The grocery store, once a mundane errand, now feels like a threat. He scans the ceiling tiles, checks the exits, and feels his heart race if someone walks too close behind him. He often leaves his cart in the aisle and walks out.

Daniel has also started to pull away from Sarah. He cannot explain it, but he feels a strange distance from her, as if a pane of glass has slid between them. He knows she is worried, and he feels guilty for worrying her, but he cannot find the words to describe what is happening inside him. He has stopped initiating sex. He feels numb, detached, as if he is watching his own life from a great distance.

At work, his performance has declined. His manager has noticed he is distracted, forgetful, and sometimes irritable with customers. Daniel used to take pride in his work—he knew the inventory, the tools, the paint colors. Now he struggles to concentrate. He has called in sick at least twice a month for the past year, often on days when he knows he will have to restock the aisles near where the collapse happened.

He has also developed a new, unsettling habit. He cannot stop researching building codes, construction accidents, and structural failures online. He spends hours reading about collapses, watching videos of falling buildings, and scanning news reports for similar incidents. Sarah has found him awake at 3 a.m., hunched over his phone, his face pale and unshaven. He tells her he is just "being prepared," but the compulsion feels beyond his control.

Daniel came to therapy because Sarah told him she is afraid for him, and for their marriage. He does not see himself as someone with a disorder. He sees himself as someone who cannot stop remembering, cannot stop scanning, and cannot stop feeling that the ground beneath him—literally—might give way at any moment.
